o: **Understanding the problem**: Rearrange s (even length n) so that s[i] ≠ s[n−1−i] for all i, returning the lexicographically smallest arrangement, or "-1" if impossible. Feasibility is purely a counting condition: some character must not occupy more than n/2 slots, i.e. max frequency ≤ n/2 (each mirror pair needs two distinct characters, so one letter can fill at most one side of every pair). "cccd" fails since 'c' appears 3 > 2 times. Starting from the sorted string gives the lexicographically smallest base; we then repair mirror conflicts locally.
k: Anti-palindrome is feasible iff no character occurs more than n/2 times.
Sorting yields the lexicographically smallest permutation; only mirror pairs (i, n−1−i) with equal characters need fixing, and swaps within the second half preserve sortedness of the first half.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort, then repair conflicting mirror pairs
a.i: In the sorted string, a conflict s[i] == s[n−1−i] means a run of equal letters straddles the middle. Swap s[i] with the smallest valid s[j] in the second half (j ≥ n/2) such that s[j] ≠ s[i] and s[n−1−j] ≠ s[i]; this fixes pair i without breaking pair n−1−j, and choosing the smallest such j keeps the result lexicographically minimal.
s: Count characters; if any exceeds n/2, return "-1".
Sort s. For each i in [0, n/2): if s[i] == s[n−1−i], scan j from n/2 upward for s[j] != s[i] and s[n−1−j] != s[i], then swap s[i] and s[j].
a.t: O(n log n + 26n) — sorting plus, for each conflicting pair, a second-half scan (amortized small)

a.i: Build the answer directly: fill the first half with the smallest available letters while ensuring the mirrored second-half slot receives a different letter — equivalently, lay out sorted letters into the first half, then fill the second half from the remaining multiset skipping any letter equal to its mirror. Same complexity, avoids post-hoc swaps but needs careful bookkeeping of remaining counts.
s: Greedily write positions 0..n/2−1 taking the smallest remaining letter whose count still allows completion (count ≤ remaining slots of its side).
Fill the second half right-to-left with the smallest remaining letter different from its mirror.
a.t: O(n log n) — heap operations over ≤26 keys plus the leftover fill

w: **Wrap-up**: Approach 1 is shorter and safer to implement under time pressure; Approach 2 shows deeper constructive understanding. The critical pitfall is the feasibility check (frequency > n/2 ⇒ "-1") — everything else follows from sorting. Another subtle point: repairs must only move characters within/across the second half so already-fixed first-half positions stay minimal. Follow-ups: count anti-palindromic permutations, or handle odd lengths (middle character unconstrained).
